INVOLUNTARY DISSOLUTION OF A CORPORATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — INVOLUNTARY DISSOLUTION OF A CORPORATION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme, Inc., a stock corporation organized under the laws of California, and describes Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1800 through 1806, and § 2000 — the General Corporation Law's involuntary-dissolution statute, which sets out the specific grounds on which a court may dissolve a corporation, which categories of directors or shareholders may petition a court for that relief, the procedure a court follows once such a petition is filed, and a statutory alternative that can avoid dissolution altogether. It is prepared with reference to Jordan Lee's relationship to Acme, Inc. Statutory ground or grounds this information sheet may relate to, if known: board deadlock.

This information sheet describes the general involuntary-dissolution rule that applies to a California corporation that has not elected close-corporation status under Cal. Corp. Code § 158. This project's existing Close Corporation — Formation Information Sheet document already describes, in its clause on deadlock and dissolution, how close-corporation status expands who may petition for dissolution beyond the general rule; this information sheet instead sets out that general rule itself — the six statutory grounds, the standing categories that apply regardless of close-corporation status, the court procedure, and the buyout alternative to dissolution — in depth that document does not.

This information sheet is educational only. It is not a verified complaint, does not itself commence any court proceeding, and does not determine whether any ground described below applies to Acme, Inc.'s circumstances, whether Jordan Lee meets any standing category described below, or whether a court would order dissolution, an alternative remedy, or no relief at all in any specific case.

STATUTORY GROUNDS FOR INVOLUNTARY DISSOLUTION
California's involuntary-dissolution statute, Cal. Corp. Code § 1800, states the grounds on which a court may order a corporation's involuntary dissolution as a list introduced by the phrase “The grounds for involuntary dissolution are that:” — six grounds in total. The first ground is that the corporation has abandoned its business for more than one year. The second is a specific form of board deadlock: an even number of directors equally divided and unable to agree on management, combined with a shareholder body itself so factionalized that it cannot elect a board with an uneven number of directors. The third ground covers internal shareholder-level dissension: two or more shareholder factions so deadlocked that the corporation's business can no longer be conducted to the shareholders' advantage, or a failure at two consecutive annual meetings to elect successor directors. The fourth ground reaches misconduct by those in control of the corporation — persistent and pervasive fraud, mismanagement, or abuse of authority, persistent unfairness toward any shareholders, or misapplication or waste of corporate property by directors or officers. The fifth ground is available only to a corporation with 35 or fewer shareholders (determined under Cal. Corp. Code § 605) and asks only whether liquidation is reasonably necessary to protect the complaining shareholder's or shareholders' rights or interests, without requiring proof of fraud, mismanagement, or deadlock. The sixth ground applies when the period for which the corporation was formed has terminated without extension. A separate subdivision of the same section excludes certain regulated corporations — those subject to California's Banking Law, Public Utilities Act, Savings Association Law, or a specified article of the Insurance Code — from the entire section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(1) The corporation has abandoned its business for more than one year."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(1), California General Corporation Law, involuntary dissolution ground: abandonment of business (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(2) The corporation has an even number of directors who are equally divided and cannot agree as to the management of its affairs, so that its business can no longer be conducted to advantage or so that there is danger that its property and business will be impaired or lost, and the holders of the voting shares of the corporation are so divided into factions that they cannot elect a board consisting of an uneven number."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(2), California General Corporation Law, involuntary dissolution ground: board deadlock (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(3) There is internal dissension and two or more factions of shareholders in the corporation are so deadlocked that its business can no longer be conducted with advantage to its shareholders or the shareholders have failed at two consecutive annual meetings at which all voting power was exercised, to elect successors to directors whose terms have expired or would have expired upon election of their successors."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(3), California General Corporation Law, involuntary dissolution ground: internal dissension and shareholder deadlock (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(4) Those in control of the corporation have been guilty of or have knowingly countenanced persistent and pervasive fraud, mismanagement or abuse of authority or persistent unfairness toward any shareholders or its property is being misapplied or wasted by its directors or officers."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(4), California General Corporation Law, involuntary dissolution ground: fraud, mismanagement, or abuse of authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(5) In the case of any corporation with 35 or fewer shareholders (determined as provided in Section 605), liquidation is reasonably necessary for the protection of the rights or interests of the complaining shareholder or shareholders."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(5), California General Corporation Law, involuntary dissolution ground: 35-or-fewer-shareholder corporations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(6) The period for which the corporation was formed has terminated without extension of such period."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(6), California General Corporation Law, involuntary dissolution ground: expiration of the corporate term (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  Known gap: Single-source disclosure: all six grounds are subdivisions of one statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1800, and are not independent of each other or of the standing categories described in this document's companion clause on standing, which are also drawn from § 1800. This clause describes only the grounds the general involuntary-dissolution statute itself enumerates; it does not describe the separate ground on which the Attorney General may sue to dissolve a corporation under Cal. Corp. Code § 1801, which rests on different conduct (offenses against the corporations statutes, fraudulent abuse of corporate privileges, and similar) and is not a shareholder- or director-initiated proceeding, and this document does not otherwise address § 1801. Nothing in this clause determines whether any specific corporation's circumstances satisfy any of these grounds.

STANDING TO PETITION FOR INVOLUNTARY DISSOLUTION — THE GENERAL RULE
Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a) identifies the persons who may file a verified complaint for a corporation's involuntary dissolution on one or more of the statute's enumerated grounds, and where that complaint must be filed: the superior court of the proper county. Four categories of petitioner are listed. The first is one-half or more of the directors then in office. The second is a shareholder or shareholders together holding shares representing not less than 33 1/3 percent of the corporation's outstanding shares (counting convertible preferred shares as converted), or of its outstanding common shares, or of its equity — excluding, in each of those three measures, shares held by anyone who personally participated in the fraud, mismanagement, or abuse-of-authority conduct described in the statute's fourth ground, and excluding any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation, for whom the same subdivision separately grants standing without regard to percentage. The third category is any shareholder at all, without regard to the size of that shareholder's holding, but only where the asserted ground is the sixth ground: that the corporation's stated term has expired without extension. The fourth category is any other person the corporation's own articles of incorporation expressly authorize to bring the action. A separate subdivision of the same section extends the statute's use of the word “shareholder” to include a beneficial owner of shares who has entered into an agreement under Cal. Corp. Code § 300 or § 706.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(1) One-half or more of the directors in office."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(1), California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution: directors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(2) A shareholder or shareholders who hold shares representing not less than 33 1 / 3 percent of (i) the total number of outstanding shares (assuming conversion of any preferred shares convertible into common shares) or (ii) the outstanding common shares or (iii) the equity of the corporation, exclusive in each case of shares owned by persons who have personally participated in any of the transactions enumerated in paragraph (4) of subdivision (b), or any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(2), California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution: shareholders holding 33 1/3 percent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(3) Any shareholder if the ground for dissolution is that the period for which the corporation was formed has terminated without extension thereof."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(3), California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution: any shareholder on the term-expiration ground (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(4) Any other person expressly authorized to do so in the articles."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(4), California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution: persons authorized in the articles (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(e) For the purposes of this section, “shareholder” includes a beneficial owner of shares who has entered into an agreement under Section 300 or 706."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(e), California General Corporation Law, the term “shareholder” includes certain beneficial owners (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  Known gap: Single-source disclosure: all four standing categories, and the beneficial-owner definition, are subdivisions of one statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1800, and are not independent of each other or of the grounds described in this document's companion clause on grounds, which are also drawn from § 1800. This clause describes only the general standing rule that applies whether or not a corporation has elected close-corporation status; it deliberately omits the close-corporation-specific expansion of the second category (to any close-corporation shareholder regardless of percentage) and the parallel close-corporation expansion of standing to petition for court supervision of a voluntary winding up under § 1904, both of which this project's existing Close Corporation — Formation Information Sheet document already covers (clause closecorp_deadlock_dissolution) and which are not repeated here. This clause also does not describe the Attorney General's separate standing to sue under § 1801, a different, non-shareholder proceeding.

FILING, INTERVENTION, RECEIVERSHIP, AND THE COURT'S DECREE
The involuntary-dissolution action begins with a verified complaint filed in the superior court of the proper county, as Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a) itself specifies. Once the action is pending, § 1800(c) gives any shareholder or creditor of the corporation — not only the original petitioner — the right to intervene in the action at any time before trial. If, at the time the complaint is filed or at any later point, the court has reasonable grounds to believe the corporation's and its shareholders' interests will suffer before the complaint can be heard and decided unless a receiver is appointed, Cal. Corp. Code § 1803 authorizes the court, on the plaintiff's application, after a noticed hearing, and upon the plaintiff's giving of security under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 566 and 567, to appoint a receiver to take over and manage the corporation's business and affairs and preserve its property pending that hearing and determination. After the hearing on the merits, Cal. Corp. Code § 1804 gives the court two distinct paths: it may decree a winding up and dissolution of the corporation if cause for that relief is shown, or — with or without ordering winding up and dissolution — it may instead make whatever orders, decrees, and injunctions in the case that justice and equity require. The statute's text does not limit that second path to any particular list of alternative orders.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) A verified complaint for involuntary dissolution of a corporation on any one or more of the grounds specified in subdivision (b) may be filed in the superior court of the proper county by any of the following persons:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a), California General Corporation Law, filing venue for an involuntary dissolution complaint (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "(c) At any time prior to the trial of the action any shareholder or creditor may intervene therein."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(c), California General Corporation Law, right of a shareholder or creditor to intervene (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1800.)
  "1803. If, at the time of the filing of a complaint for involuntary dissolution or at any time thereafter, the court has reasonable grounds to believe that unless a receiver of the corporation is appointed the interests of the corporation and its shareholders will suffer pending the hearing and determination of the complaint, upon the application of the plaintiff, and after a hearing upon such notice to the corporation as the court may direct and upon the giving of security pursuant to Sections 566 and 567 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may appoint a receiver to take over and manage the business and affairs of the corporation and to preserve its property pending the hearing and determination of the complaint for dissolution. (Added by Stats. 1975, Ch. 682.)"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1803, California General Corporation Law, pendente lite receiver in an involuntary dissolution action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1803.)
  "1804. After hearing the court may decree a winding up and dissolution of the corporation if cause therefor is shown or, with or without winding up and dissolution, may make such orders and decrees and issue such injunctions in the case as justice and equity require. (Added by Stats. 1975, Ch. 682.)"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1804, California General Corporation Law, the court's post-hearing decree power (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1804.)
  Known gap: Source-independence disclosure: the quotations from § 1800(a) and § 1800(c) are subdivisions of the same statutory section as the grounds and standing categories described in this document's other clauses and are not independent of them. The quotations from § 1803 and § 1804 are each drawn from independently numbered sections of the same chapter (Chapter 18, Involuntary Dissolution) and are independent of § 1800 and of each other for source-diversity purposes, though all three sections were adopted together as part of one 1975 enactment (Stats. 1975, Ch. 682), which is disclosed here rather than presented as unrelated corroboration. This clause does not catalog every procedural detail Chapter 18 addresses — for example, § 1801's Attorney General dissolution action, and §§ 1807 through 1809's creditor-claims-bar, final-decree, and Secretary of State filing provisions, which govern the later and more granular mechanics of a completed dissolution — and is not exhaustive of the chapter.

PROVISIONAL DIRECTOR AS AN INTERIM REMEDY FOR BOARD DEADLOCK
Where the asserted ground for an involuntary-dissolution complaint is board deadlock — the ground Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(2) defines as an evenly divided board that cannot agree on management, coupled with a shareholder body too factionalized to elect an uneven-numbered board — Cal. Corp. Code § 1802 gives the court a specific interim option: rather than proceeding only toward dissolution, the court may appoint a provisional director. Section 1802 does not create its own separate standard for that appointment; it incorporates by reference the provisional-director procedure of Cal. Corp. Code § 308(c), which governs the powers, term, and other conditions of a provisional director once appointed. This option exists specifically inside the involuntary-dissolution proceeding, for the deadlock ground — the statute's text ties it only to § 1800(b)(2), not to the statute's other five grounds for dissolution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "1802. If the ground for the complaint for involuntary dissolution of the corporation is a deadlock in the board as set forth in subdivision (b)(2) of Section 1800, the court may appoint a provisional director. The provisions of subdivision (c) of Section 308 apply to any such provisional director so appointed. (Amended by Stats. 1977, Ch. 235.)"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1802, California General Corporation Law, provisional director as an alternative to dissolution for board deadlock (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1802.)
  Known gap: Independent-source disclosure: § 1802 is an independently numbered section of Chapter 18, separate from § 1800, § 1803, and § 1804 cited elsewhere in this document. This clause quotes and describes only § 1802's incorporation of § 308(c) by cross-reference; it does not itself quote or independently re-verify the text of § 308, which this project's existing Close Corporation — Formation Information Sheet document already quotes and verifies (as § 308(a)) for a different, narrower point — that the provisional-director remedy generally is not limited to close corporations. This clause's point is different and additional: that within an involuntary-dissolution action specifically, § 1802 makes a provisional director an available alternative to full dissolution when the ground is board deadlock. This clause does not evaluate whether appointing a provisional director, rather than proceeding toward dissolution, would be appropriate in any specific case.

COURT SUPERVISION OF THE WINDING-UP PROCESS
When a court orders a corporation's involuntary winding up under Cal. Corp. Code § 1804, that order itself marks the start of the winding-up proceeding, as § 1805(a) states. From that point, § 1805(b) puts the board itself in charge of conducting the winding up, but only subject to the supervision of the court, unless the court instead appoints other persons, on a showing of good cause, to conduct it; either the board or any court-appointed substitute may exercise their powers through the corporation's executive officers without needing a separate court order for each act. Under § 1805(c), once winding up has commenced the corporation must stop carrying on business except to the extent winding up itself requires, or as needed to preserve goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of the business or its assets, and the directors must mail written notice of the winding-up proceeding to all shareholders and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the corporation's records. Cal. Corp. Code § 1806 then defines what the court's ongoing jurisdiction over that winding up covers, including the presentation and barring of creditors' claims, the determination of shareholders' rights to the corporation's assets, the settling of the accounts of the persons conducting the winding up, the filling of board vacancies, staying other suits against the corporation, and — as one specific example — removing a director for dishonesty, misconduct, neglect, or abuse of trust in conducting the winding up, with the further power either to enjoin that director's re-election or to appoint a replacement director directly rather than ordering a new election.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) Involuntary proceedings for winding up a corporation commence when the order for winding up is entered under Section 1804."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1805(a), California General Corporation Law, commencement of an involuntary winding-up proceeding (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1805.)
  "(b) When an involuntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the board shall conduct the winding up of the affairs of the corporation, subject to the supervision of the court, unless other persons are appointed by the court, on good cause shown, to conduct the winding up. The directors or such other persons may, subject to any restrictions imposed by the court, exercise all their powers through the executive officers without any order of court."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1805(b), California General Corporation Law, the board conducts winding up subject to court supervision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1805.)
  "(c) When an involuntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the corporation shall cease to carry on business except to the extent necessary for the beneficial winding up thereof and except during such period as the board may deem necessary to preserve the corporation’s goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of its business or assets, or both, in whole or in part. The directors shall cause written notice of the commencement of the proceeding for involuntary winding up to be given by mail to all shareholders and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the records of the corporation, unless the order for winding up has been stayed by appeal therefrom or otherwise or the proceeding or the execution of the order has been enjoined."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1805(c), California General Corporation Law, restriction on carrying on business and notice to shareholders and creditors during winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1805.)
  "1806. When an involuntary proceeding for winding up has been commenced, the jurisdiction of the court includes:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1806, California General Corporation Law, the scope of the court's jurisdiction during involuntary winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1806.)
  "(g) The removal of any director if it appears that the director has been guilty of dishonesty, misconduct, neglect or abuse of trust in conducting the winding up or if the director is unable to act. The court may order an election to fill the vacancy so caused, and may enjoin, for such time as it considers proper, the reelection of the director so removed; or the court, in lieu of ordering an election, may appoint a director to fill the vacancy caused by such removal. Any director so appointed by the court shall serve until the next annual meeting of shareholders or until a successor is elected or appointed."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1806(g), California General Corporation Law, the court's power to remove a director during winding up (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1806.)
  Known gap: Independent-source disclosure: § 1805 and § 1806 are each independently numbered sections of Chapter 18, separate from § 1800, § 1802, § 1803, and § 1804 cited elsewhere in this document, and from each other, though all were enacted as part of the same 1975 chapter (Stats. 1975, Ch. 682). Within this clause, § 1805(a), (b), and (c) are subdivisions of one section and are not independent of each other; the § 1806 introductory clause and § 1806(g) quoted below are similarly subdivisions of one section and not independent of each other. This clause covers only the subdivisions of § 1805 and § 1806 that describe the general shape of court-supervised winding up; it summarizes rather than quotes § 1806's remaining specific jurisdictional grants (subdivisions (a) through (f) and (h) through (l)) for length, and omits §§ 1807 through 1809, which separately govern the creditor-claims-bar notice procedure, the final decree of dissolution, and the requirement to file that decree with the Secretary of State. This clause does not evaluate whether court-supervised winding up, rather than some other outcome, would apply to any specific proceeding.

BUYOUT ALTERNATIVE TO DISSOLUTION
A separate statute, outside Chapter 18, gives the corporation itself — or, if the corporation does not act, its own majority shareholders — a way to stop an involuntary-dissolution action without a dissolution ever being decreed. Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(a) provides that, subject to any contrary provision in the articles, in any suit for involuntary dissolution the corporation or, if it does not elect to purchase, the holders of 50 percent or more of the corporation's voting power (the statute's defined “purchasing parties”) may avoid the corporation's dissolution and the appointment of any receiver by purchasing for cash, at fair value, the shares owned by the plaintiffs in the dissolution action (the statute's defined “moving parties”). Fair value under § 2000(a) is measured on a liquidation-value basis as of the valuation date, but taking into account the possibility of selling the entire business as a going concern rather than piecemeal. Any damages the moving parties owe the purchasing parties for breaching an agreement by initiating the dissolution suit may be deducted from what the purchasing parties owe for the shares — except where the dissolution ground is § 1800(b)(4)'s fraud, mismanagement, or abuse-of-authority ground, in which case § 2000(a) does not allow that deduction. If the purchasing parties elect to buy the shares but cannot agree with the moving parties on fair value, § 2000(b) requires them to post a bond covering the moving parties' reasonably estimated litigation expenses, after which the court stays the dissolution proceeding and itself proceeds to fix fair value. Under § 2000(c), that valuation is made by three court-appointed disinterested appraisers, whose award, once confirmed by the court, is final and conclusive on all parties, subject to appeal, and the court's resulting decree provides for winding up and dissolution to proceed unless the purchasing parties pay for the shares within the time the decree specifies. Section 2000(f) fixes the valuation date, for an involuntary-dissolution suit under § 1800, as the date that suit was commenced, subject to the court's power to designate a different date for good cause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) Subject to any contrary provision in the articles, which may include a reference to a separate written agreement between two or more shareholders pertaining to the purchase of shares: In any suit for involuntary dissolution, or in any proceeding for voluntary dissolution initiated by the vote of shareholders representing only 50 percent of the voting power, the corporation or, if it does not elect to purchase, the holders of 50 percent or more of the voting power of the corporation (the “purchasing parties”) may avoid the dissolution of the corporation and the appointment of any receiver by purchasing for cash the shares owned by the plaintiffs or by the shareholders so initiating the proceeding (the “moving parties”) at their fair value. The fair value shall be determined on the basis of the liquidation value as of the valuation date but taking into account the possibility, if any, of sale of the entire business as a going concern in a liquidation. In fixing the value, the amount of any damages resulting if the initiation of the dissolution is a breach by any moving party or parties of an agreement with the purchasing party or parties may be deducted from the amount payable to the moving party or parties, unless the ground for dissolution is that specified in paragraph (4) of subdivision (b) of Section 1800. The election of the corporation to purchase may be made by the approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152) excluding shares held by the moving parties."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(a), California General Corporation Law, the buyout alternative to dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2000.)
  "(b) If the purchasing parties (1) elect to purchase the shares owned by the moving parties, and (2) are unable to agree with the moving parties upon the fair value of those shares, and (3) give bond with sufficient security to pay the estimated reasonable expenses (including attorneys’ fees) of the moving parties if those expenses are recoverable under subdivision (c), the court upon application of the purchasing parties, either in the pending action or in a proceeding initiated in the superior court of the proper county by the purchasing parties in the case of a voluntary election to wind up and dissolve, shall stay the winding up and dissolution proceeding and shall proceed to ascertain and fix the fair value of the shares owned by the moving parties."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(b), California General Corporation Law, bond and stay procedure when the parties cannot agree on fair value (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2000.)
  "(c) The court shall appoint three disinterested appraisers to appraise the fair value of the shares owned by the moving parties, and shall make an order referring the matter to the appraisers so appointed for the purpose of ascertaining the value. The order shall prescribe the time and manner of producing evidence, if evidence is required. The award of the appraisers or of a majority of them, when confirmed by the court, shall be final and conclusive upon all parties. The court shall enter a decree, which shall provide in the alternative for winding up and dissolution of the corporation unless payment is made for the shares within the time specified by the decree. If the purchasing parties do not make payment for the shares within the time specified, judgment shall be entered against them and the surety or sureties on the bond for the amount of the expenses (including attorneys’ fees) of the moving parties. Any shareholder aggrieved by the action of the court may appeal the court’s decision."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(c), California General Corporation Law, court-appointed appraisers and the resulting decree (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2000.)
  "(f) For the purposes of this section, the valuation date shall be (1) in the case of a suit for involuntary dissolution under Section 1800, the date upon which that action was commenced, or (2) in the case of a proceeding for voluntary dissolution initiated by the vote of shareholders representing only 50 percent of the voting power, the date upon which that proceeding was initiated. However, in either case the court may, upon the hearing of a motion by any party, and for good cause shown, designate some other date as the valuation date."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(f), California General Corporation Law, the valuation date for a Section 1800 involuntary dissolution suit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2000.)
  Known gap: Independent-source disclosure: § 2000 is codified in a different chapter of the General Corporation Law (Chapter 20, General Provisions Relating to Dissolution, §§ 2000–2011) than § 1800 and the other Chapter 18 sections cited elsewhere in this document (Chapter 18, Involuntary Dissolution, §§ 1800–1809), and is independent of them for source-diversity purposes, though it cross-references § 1800 directly and both chapters were enacted in the same 1975 legislation (Stats. 1975, Ch. 682). Within this clause, § 2000(a), (b), (c), and (f) are subdivisions of one section and are not independent of each other. This clause does not describe § 2000(d) (payment mechanics once value is fixed) or § 2000(e) (the beneficial-owner definition, which parallels § 1800(e)) in the same depth, and does not evaluate whether this buyout alternative would be available, elected, or advantageous in any specific dissolution proceeding — that depends on the corporation's articles, the specific ground alleged, and facts about value that this clause does not address.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — INVOLUNTARY DISSOLUTION OF A CORPORATION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet regarding Acme, Inc. was prepared by Jordan Lee, whose approximate ownership or membership interest in Acme, Inc., if known, is 10%.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

It is not a verified complaint, a demand, or any other court filing, does not determine whether any ground or standing category described in it applies to Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee, and does not constitute legal advice. The current statutory text is published by the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov).]

It is not a verified complaint, does not itself commence any court proceeding, and does not determine whether any ground described below applies to Acme, Inc.'s circumstances, whether Jordan Lee meets any standing category described below, or whether a court would order dissolution, an alternative remedy, or no relief at all in any specific case.

California's involuntary-dissolution statute, Cal. Corp. Code § 1800, states the grounds on which a court may order a corporation's involuntary dissolution as a list introduced by the phrase “The grounds for involuntary dissolution are that:” — six grounds in total. The first ground is that the corporation has abandoned its business for more than one year. The second is a specific form of board deadlock: an even number of directors equally divided and unable to agree on management, combined with a shareholder body itself so factionalized that it cannot elect a board with an uneven number of directors. The third ground covers internal shareholder-level dissension: two or more shareholder factions so deadlocked that the corporation's business can no longer be conducted to the shareholders' advantage, or a failure at two consecutive annual meetings to elect successor directors. The fourth ground reaches misconduct by those in control of the corporation — persistent and pervasive fraud, mismanagement, or abuse of authority, persistent unfairness toward any shareholders, or misapplication or waste of corporate property by directors or officers. The fifth ground is available only to a corporation with 35 or fewer shareholders (determined under Cal. Corp. Code § 605) and asks only whether liquidation is reasonably necessary to protect the complaining shareholder's or shareholders' rights or interests, without requiring proof of fraud, mismanagement, or deadlock. The sixth ground applies when the period for which the corporation was formed has terminated without extension. A separate subdivision of the same section excludes certain regulated corporations — those subject to California's Banking Law, Public Utilities Act, Savings Association Law, or a specified article of the Insurance Code — from the entire section.

expectedJSON.body: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a) identifies the persons who may file a verified complaint for a corporation's involuntary dissolution on one or more of the statute's enumerated grounds, and where that complaint must be filed: the superior court of the proper county. Four categories of petitioner are listed. The first is one-half or more of the directors then in office. The second is a shareholder or shareholders together holding shares representing not less than 33 1/3 percent of the corporation's outstanding shares (counting convertible preferred shares as converted), or of its outstanding common shares, or of its equity — excluding, in each of those three measures, shares held by anyone who personally participated in the fraud, mismanagement, or abuse-of-authority conduct described in the statute's fourth ground, and excluding any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation, for whom the same subdivision separately grants standing without regard to percentage. The third category is any shareholder at all, without regard to the size of that shareholder's holding, but only where the asserted ground is the sixth ground: that the corporation's stated term has expired without extension. The fourth category is any other person the corporation's own articles of incorporation expressly authorize to bring the action. A separate subdivision of the same section extends the statute's use of the word “shareholder” to include a beneficial owner of shares who has entered into an agreement under Cal. Corp. Code § 300 or § 706.

expectedJSON.body: The involuntary-dissolution action begins with a verified complaint filed in the superior court of the proper county, as Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a) itself specifies. Once the action is pending, § 1800(c) gives any shareholder or creditor of the corporation — not only the original petitioner — the right to intervene in the action at any time before trial. If, at the time the complaint is filed or at any later point, the court has reasonable grounds to believe the corporation's and its shareholders' interests will suffer before the complaint can be heard and decided unless a receiver is appointed, Cal. Corp. Code § 1803 authorizes the court, on the plaintiff's application, after a noticed hearing, and upon the plaintiff's giving of security under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 566 and 567, to appoint a receiver to take over and manage the corporation's business and affairs and preserve its property pending that hearing and determination. After the hearing on the merits, Cal. Corp. Code § 1804 gives the court two distinct paths: it may decree a winding up and dissolution of the corporation if cause for that relief is shown, or — with or without ordering winding up and dissolution — it may instead make whatever orders, decrees, and injunctions in the case that justice and equity require. The statute's text does not limit that second path to any particular list of alternative orders.

citations.quote: (a) A verified complaint for involuntary dissolution of a corporation on any one or more of the grounds specified in subdivision (b) may be filed in the superior court of the proper county by any of the following persons:

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, right of a shareholder or creditor to intervene
citations.quote: (c) At any time prior to the trial of the action any shareholder or creditor may intervene therein.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, pendente lite receiver in an involuntary dissolution action
citations.quote: 1803. If, at the time of the filing of a complaint for involuntary dissolution or at any time thereafter, the court has reasonable grounds to believe that unless a receiver of the corporation is appointed the interests of the corporation and its shareholders will suffer pending the hearing and determination of the complaint, upon the application of the plaintiff, and after a hearing upon such notice to the corporation as the court may direct and upon the giving of security pursuant to Sections 566 and 567 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may appoint a receiver to take over and manage the business and affairs of the corporation and to preserve its property pending the hearing and determination of the complaint for dissolution. (Added by Stats. 1975, Ch. 682.)

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the court's post-hearing decree power
citations.quote: 1804. After hearing the court may decree a winding up and dissolution of the corporation if cause therefor is shown or, with or without winding up and dissolution, may make such orders and decrees and issue such injunctions in the case as justice and equity require. (Added by Stats. 1975, Ch. 682.)

expectedJSON.body: Where the asserted ground for an involuntary-dissolution complaint is board deadlock — the ground Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(2) defines as an evenly divided board that cannot agree on management, coupled with a shareholder body too factionalized to elect an uneven-numbered board — Cal. Corp. Code § 1802 gives the court a specific interim option: rather than proceeding only toward dissolution, the court may appoint a provisional director. Section 1802 does not create its own separate standard for that appointment; it incorporates by reference the provisional-director procedure of Cal. Corp. Code § 308(c), which governs the powers, term, and other conditions of a provisional director once appointed. This option exists specifically inside the involuntary-dissolution proceeding, for the deadlock ground — the statute's text ties it only to § 1800(b)(2), not to the statute's other five grounds for dissolution.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, provisional director as an alternative to dissolution for board deadlock
citations.quote: 1802. If the ground for the complaint for involuntary dissolution of the corporation is a deadlock in the board as set forth in subdivision (b)(2) of Section 1800, the court may appoint a provisional director. The provisions of subdivision (c) of Section 308 apply to any such provisional director so appointed. (Amended by Stats. 1977, Ch. 235.)

expectedJSON.gap: Independent-source disclosure: § 1802 is an independently numbered section of Chapter 18, separate from § 1800, § 1803, and § 1804 cited elsewhere in this document. This clause quotes and describes only § 1802's incorporation of § 308(c) by cross-reference; it does not itself quote or independently re-verify the text of § 308, which this project's existing Close Corporation — Formation Information Sheet document already quotes and verifies (as § 308(a)) for a different, narrower point — that the provisional-director remedy generally is not limited to close corporations. This clause's point is different and additional: that within an involuntary-dissolution action specifically, § 1802 makes a provisional director an available alternative to full dissolution when the ground is board deadlock. This clause does not evaluate whether appointing a provisional director, rather than proceeding toward dissolution, would be appropriate in any specific case.

expectedJSON.body: When a court orders a corporation's involuntary winding up under Cal. Corp. Code § 1804, that order itself marks the start of the winding-up proceeding, as § 1805(a) states. From that point, § 1805(b) puts the board itself in charge of conducting the winding up, but only subject to the supervision of the court, unless the court instead appoints other persons, on a showing of good cause, to conduct it; either the board or any court-appointed substitute may exercise their powers through the corporation's executive officers without needing a separate court order for each act. Under § 1805(c), once winding up has commenced the corporation must stop carrying on business except to the extent winding up itself requires, or as needed to preserve goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of the business or its assets, and the directors must mail written notice of the winding-up proceeding to all shareholders and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the corporation's records. Cal. Corp. Code § 1806 then defines what the court's ongoing jurisdiction over that winding up covers, including the presentation and barring of creditors' claims, the determination of shareholders' rights to the corporation's assets, the settling of the accounts of the persons conducting the winding up, the filling of board vacancies, staying other suits against the corporation, and — as one specific example — removing a director for dishonesty, misconduct, neglect, or abuse of trust in conducting the winding up, with the further power either to enjoin that director's re-election or to appoint a replacement director directly rather than ordering a new election.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, commencement of an involuntary winding-up proceeding
citations.quote: (a) Involuntary proceedings for winding up a corporation commence when the order for winding up is entered under Section 1804.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the board conducts winding up subject to court supervision
citations.quote: (b) When an involuntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the board shall conduct the winding up of the affairs of the corporation, subject to the supervision of the court, unless other persons are appointed by the court, on good cause shown, to conduct the winding up. The directors or such other persons may, subject to any restrictions imposed by the court, exercise all their powers through the executive officers without any order of court.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, restriction on carrying on business and notice to shareholders and creditors during winding up
citations.quote: (c) When an involuntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the corporation shall cease to carry on business except to the extent necessary for the beneficial winding up thereof and except during such period as the board may deem necessary to preserve the corporation’s goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of its business or assets, or both, in whole or in part. The directors shall cause written notice of the commencement of the proceeding for involuntary winding up to be given by mail to all shareholders and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the records of the corporation, unless the order for winding up has been stayed by appeal therefrom or otherwise or the proceeding or the execution of the order has been enjoined.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the scope of the court's jurisdiction during involuntary winding up
citations.quote: 1806. When an involuntary proceeding for winding up has been commenced, the jurisdiction of the court includes:

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the court's power to remove a director during winding up
citations.quote: (g) The removal of any director if it appears that the director has been guilty of dishonesty, misconduct, neglect or abuse of trust in conducting the winding up or if the director is unable to act. The court may order an election to fill the vacancy so caused, and may enjoin, for such time as it considers proper, the reelection of the director so removed; or the court, in lieu of ordering an election, may appoint a director to fill the vacancy caused by such removal. Any director so appointed by the court shall serve until the next annual meeting of shareholders or until a successor is elected or appointed.

Within this clause, § 1805(a), (b), and (c) are subdivisions of one section and are not independent of each other; the § 1806 introductory clause and § 1806(g) quoted below are similarly subdivisions of one section and not independent of each other. This clause covers only the subdivisions of § 1805 and § 1806 that describe the general shape of court-supervised winding up; it summarizes rather than quotes § 1806's remaining specific jurisdictional grants (subdivisions (a) through (f) and (h) through (l)) for length, and omits §§ 1807 through 1809, which separately govern the creditor-claims-bar notice procedure, the final decree of dissolution, and the requirement to file that decree with the Secretary of State. expectedJSON.body: A separate statute, outside Chapter 18, gives the corporation itself — or, if the corporation does not act, its own majority shareholders — a way to stop an involuntary-dissolution action without a dissolution ever being decreed. Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(a) provides that, subject to any contrary provision in the articles, in any suit for involuntary dissolution the corporation or, if it does not elect to purchase, the holders of 50 percent or more of the corporation's voting power (the statute's defined “purchasing parties”) may avoid the corporation's dissolution and the appointment of any receiver by purchasing for cash, at fair value, the shares owned by the plaintiffs in the dissolution action (the statute's defined “moving parties”). Fair value under § 2000(a) is measured on a liquidation-value basis as of the valuation date, but taking into account the possibility of selling the entire business as a going concern rather than piecemeal. Any damages the moving parties owe the purchasing parties for breaching an agreement by initiating the dissolution suit may be deducted from what the purchasing parties owe for the shares — except where the dissolution ground is § 1800(b)(4)'s fraud, mismanagement, or abuse-of-authority ground, in which case § 2000(a) does not allow that deduction. If the purchasing parties elect to buy the shares but cannot agree with the moving parties on fair value, § 2000(b) requires them to post a bond covering the moving parties' reasonably estimated litigation expenses, after which the court stays the dissolution proceeding and itself proceeds to fix fair value. Under § 2000(c), that valuation is made by three court-appointed disinterested appraisers, whose award, once confirmed by the court, is final and conclusive on all parties, subject to appeal, and the court's resulting decree provides for winding up and dissolution to proceed unless the purchasing parties pay for the shares within the time the decree specifies. Section 2000(f) fixes the valuation date, for an involuntary-dissolution suit under § 1800, as the date that suit was commenced, subject to the court's power to designate a different date for good cause.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the buyout alternative to dissolution
citations.quote: (a) Subject to any contrary provision in the articles, which may include a reference to a separate written agreement between two or more shareholders pertaining to the purchase of shares: In any suit for involuntary dissolution, or in any proceeding for voluntary dissolution initiated by the vote of shareholders representing only 50 percent of the voting power, the corporation or, if it does not elect to purchase, the holders of 50 percent or more of the voting power of the corporation (the “purchasing parties”) may avoid the dissolution of the corporation and the appointment of any receiver by purchasing for cash the shares owned by the plaintiffs or by the shareholders so initiating the proceeding (the “moving parties”) at their fair value. The fair value shall be determined on the basis of the liquidation value as of the valuation date but taking into account the possibility, if any, of sale of the entire business as a going concern in a liquidation. In fixing the value, the amount of any damages resulting if the initiation of the dissolution is a breach by any moving party or parties of an agreement with the purchasing party or parties may be deducted from the amount payable to the moving party or parties, unless the ground for dissolution is that specified in paragraph (4) of subdivision (b) of Section 1800. The election of the corporation to purchase may be made by the approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152) excluding shares held by the moving parties.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, bond and stay procedure when the parties cannot agree on fair value
citations.quote: (b) If the purchasing parties (1) elect to purchase the shares owned by the moving parties, and (2) are unable to agree with the moving parties upon the fair value of those shares, and (3) give bond with sufficient security to pay the estimated reasonable expenses (including attorneys’ fees) of the moving parties if those expenses are recoverable under subdivision (c), the court upon application of the purchasing parties, either in the pending action or in a proceeding initiated in the superior court of the proper county by the purchasing parties in the case of a voluntary election to wind up and dissolve, shall stay the winding up and dissolution proceeding and shall proceed to ascertain and fix the fair value of the shares owned by the moving parties.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, court-appointed appraisers and the resulting decree
citations.quote: (c) The court shall appoint three disinterested appraisers to appraise the fair value of the shares owned by the moving parties, and shall make an order referring the matter to the appraisers so appointed for the purpose of ascertaining the value. The order shall prescribe the time and manner of producing evidence, if evidence is required. The award of the appraisers or of a majority of them, when confirmed by the court, shall be final and conclusive upon all parties. The court shall enter a decree, which shall provide in the alternative for winding up and dissolution of the corporation unless payment is made for the shares within the time specified by the decree. If the purchasing parties do not make payment for the shares within the time specified, judgment shall be entered against them and the surety or sureties on the bond for the amount of the expenses (including attorneys’ fees) of the moving parties. Any shareholder aggrieved by the action of the court may appeal the court’s decision.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the valuation date for a Section 1800 involuntary dissolution suit
citations.quote: (f) For the purposes of this section, the valuation date shall be (1) in the case of a suit for involuntary dissolution under Section 1800, the date upon which that action was commenced, or (2) in the case of a proceeding for voluntary dissolution initiated by the vote of shareholders representing only 50 percent of the voting power, the date upon which that proceeding was initiated. However, in either case the court may, upon the hearing of a motion by any party, and for good cause shown, designate some other date as the valuation date.

Within this clause, § 2000(a), (b), (c), and (f) are subdivisions of one section and are not independent of each other. This clause does not describe § 2000(d) (payment mechanics once value is fixed) or § 2000(e) (the beneficial-owner definition, which parallels § 1800(e)) in the same depth, and does not evaluate whether this buyout alternative would be available, elected, or advantageous in any specific dissolution proceeding — that depends on the corporation's articles, the specific ground alleged, and facts about value that this clause does not address.
